balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

propertyEbitda.title: Adjusted Property EBITDA by property
propertyEbitda.content:
Adjusted Property EBITDA is each resort's operating profit before corporate overhead, stock-based compensation and other non-property items -- the figure management uses to compare properties against each other and against competitors.

For Las Vegas Sands: the five Macao properties collapsed to a near-zero or negative combined EBITDA in FY2022 (border closures, zero-COVID policy) and have been rebuilding since reopening; Marina Bay Sands never closed and has grown through the period, which is why its share of the mix looks structurally higher than pre-pandemic.

What to watch:

  • Whether the Macao properties as a group are closing the gap to pre-pandemic (FY2019) levels
  • Which Macao property is driving the recovery -- Londoner (the newest, most capital) versus the older Sands/Plaza
  • Marina Bay Sands' EBITDA margin versus Macao's -- Singapore carries a casino tax and labour cost structure Macao does not

macaoVsMbs.title: Macao vs Marina Bay Sands
macaoVsMbs.content:
The five Macao properties summed, against the single Marina Bay Sands property in Singapore -- the two markets behind the group total.

For Las Vegas Sands: Macao is the larger market by property count and mass-market potential, but Marina Bay Sands has been the more consistent earner since its 2022-2023 reopening; the DCF's growth case leans on Macao closing that gap as Chinese visitation normalises and the Londoner ramps.

What to watch:

  • Macao's EBITDA growing faster than MBS's (the recovery thesis), not just growing
  • Any renewed Macao travel restriction or junket-related disruption
  • MBS capacity -- it is land-constrained in Singapore, so its growth ceiling is closer than Macao's

revpar.title: RevPAR by property
revpar.content:
RevPAR (revenue per available room) is hotel room revenue divided by available room-nights -- occupancy times average daily rate in one number, in US dollars per room-night.

For Las Vegas Sands: hotel rooms are the draw that brings gaming customers onto the property, so RevPAR is a leading indicator of footfall, not just a hotel-segment metric; Marina Bay Sands' RevPAR runs several times any Macao property's because Singapore commands a luxury-leisure rate Macao's mass-market hotels do not.

What to watch:

  • Londoner and Parisian RevPAR trending toward Venetian's (the newer builds maturing)
  • Seasonality -- Chinese New Year and summer quarters run well above the annual average
  • RevPAR growth outrunning or lagging the broader Macao visitation recovery

rollingChipWin.title: Rolling chip win %
rollingChipWin.content:
Rolling chip win % is VIP/premium baccarat table winnings as a percentage of the rolling chip volume wagered -- the house edge actually realised, which varies quarter to quarter around a theoretical average purely by chance (small-sample variance on high-stakes play).

For Las Vegas Sands: a property printing an unusually high or low win% in one quarter is not a change in the business -- it is the reason analysts normalise reported EBITDA for hold before comparing quarters.

What to watch:

  • Multi-quarter average reverting toward the theoretical 2.7-3.3% range
  • Rolling chip volume itself (the underlying VIP demand), not the win% noise around it
  • Sands Macao's smaller, more volatile VIP base swinging further than the larger properties

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Las Vegas Sands Corp.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
